nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What percentage of the Ile-de-France region is urbanized and how does that relate to the overall French population?
nodes.answer: 20% of the Ile-de-France region is urbanized, housing 18% of the total French population.
nodes.paragraph: We hypothesised that toads liv - ing in habitats impacted by human land use would differ in morphology. We predict that individuals from urban habi - tats will be larger and show relatively longer limbs allow - ing them to overcome landscape barriers. Animals from more open, agricultural habitats, for example, could be expected to be larger for physiological reasons (desiccation avoidance) as suggested higher. We further predict that the responses of males and females will be different because of the difference in reproductive behaviour with males having longer forelimbs due to their role in amplexus and females having larger bodies due to their investment in eggs. Methods Study area The Ile-de-France region is one of the France S smallest regions with 12 12 km2 equalling only 2.2% of the total surface area. Yet, 20% of the territory is urbanised and houses 18% of the total French population. A further 53% of the territory is agricultural and 23% is made up of forests, including the major forests of Rambouillet and Fontaineb - leau (La pr fecture et les services de I tat en r gion 2024 ; ONF 2024 ).

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What method was used for subgroup analysis in the study?
nodes.answer: Randomly selected groups were used for subgroup analysis involving urban and reference sites.
nodes.paragraph: Considering the nature of our data, we performed a subgroup analysis using randomly selected groups for the urban and reference sites to compare similar samples. We used S rensen (incidence-based) and Bray-Curtis (abundance-based) cluster analyses and found that the urban bird community composition is better explained by the vegetation cover than by the proximity to the reference sites. We confirmed this association with the results of the GLM, showing a statistically significant association with the vegetation cover. Our results are relevant in terms of urban design, considering that promoting the improvement of vegetation in cities could potentially help avian communities in these changing environments. The level of socio-economic advantage for every survey respondent was calculated according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA) [18]. The SEIFA is a group of four indexes developed by the ABS that ranks the geographic areas in Australia according to their relative socio-economic advan- tage and disadvantage. The Index of Relative Socio-eco- nomic Advantage and Disadvantage (IRSAD) was applied to each survey respondent S reported residential postcode (geo- graphic area) and each respondent was assigned a SEIFA decile score (1 10).

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: According to the study, how many factors were selected to guide the Multi-Criteria Analysis, and what is one of these factors?
nodes.answer: Nine factors were selected for the MCA, one of which is population density.
nodes.paragraph: The MCA serves as a powerful method of determining spatial suitability (Bakolo et al. 2024 ; Gelan 2021 ). We selected nine factors namely population density, proximity to roads, Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), proximity to existing green spaces, land cover types, proximity to water bodies, nitrogen dioxide concen - trations, slope, and elevation, to be used as criteria for the MCA. These factors are considered key to building a model that optimally reflects the social and ecological role of green spaces and their accessibility (Bakolo et al. 2024 ; Gelan 2021 ; Natural England 2010 ). We then assigned weights to the criteria based on the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), before computing suitability in ArcGIS Pro. The model depicting the performed GIS procedures is displayed (Fig. 2). Data acquisition and processing We accomplished all processes for obtaining NDVI, land cover, nitrogen dioxide, and elevation data in Google Earth Engine. We opted for data spanning from June to September 2023, ensuring cloud coverage of less than or equal to 5% and reducing the collected images to their respective means.
